newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Penniless depositors vow new Albania port protest.
newsitem.headline: Penniless depositors vow new Albania port protest.

text.p: Penniless Albanians who took on police in this port city vowed to stage a second day of protests on Thursday to press for the return of money trapped in failed investment funds and the government's resignation.

"We'll be back again tomorrow," said one marcher leaving for home after Tuesday's day-long protests against President Sali Berisha. "People will come from villages around here too. We'll keep coming back until this government goes."
The Interior Ministry said three protesters and three policemen had been slightly injured.

The protest, confined to Vlore, was the first in the Balkan country since investors enraged by the collapse of pyramid schemes set fire last month to public buildings in several cities. More than 150 people have since been arrested.
The latest unrest was prompted by the collapse of the Gjallica scheme popular in southern Albania.
Experts and opposition leaders say the downfall of other, bigger investment firms is inevitable and could pitch Europe's poorest country into uncontrollable violence.
Police firing in the air and equipped with water cannon and dogs tried twice on Wednesday to disperse up to 7,000 protesters denouncing Berisha and his rightist government.
After nightfall, exhausted officers allowed marchers to take control of a palm-lined boulevard, where earlier the two sides had pitched rocks at each other and shots had rung out.
Some police, who surely had money of their own tied up in the schemes, embraced protesters and swapped cigarettes. Others beat and tried to arrest demonstrators late into the evening.
Demonstrators for good measure smashed billboards promoting investment firms whose promises of quick returns have drawn in savings from virtually every family in post-Communist Albania.

"Let the president we defended in this square six years ago when he brought democracy come here with his ministers and the heads of those companies," said protester Kastriot Janushi. "Let him explain what happened. I haven't a penny to my name."
Tirana and other towns were calm, but with increased police patrols.
Local people say as much as $2 billion might be invested in pyramid schemes, which blossomed across post-communist Albania.
Investors in two other failed companies have already begun receiving refunds of between 50 and 60 percent of their deposits, although procedures at payout points were chaotic.
Berisha's Democratic Party was returned to power in general elections last May pronounced flawed by Western observers.
He has pledged to ease the losses of destitute families and denies he failed to warn investors about pyramid schemes, which must attract new investors to pay interest for existing ones.

The head of the International Monetary Fund, Michel Camdessus, told France's RFI Radio the schemes were "a catastrophe for poor people...This will cost the country dearly but it is not end of Albania's transition to a market economy."
The Socialist Party, backbone of the opposition Forum for Democracy grouping, said the Vlore protest was a futile attempt by the government to stay in power through intimidation.

"When you are dealing with money you can't keep Albanians intimidated for long," Socialist leader Rexhep Mejdani told Reuters. "You can intimidate people for a day, a week or a month... but I'm afraid in the end they will explode."
